question: An ASP.NET Core app keeps the current customer's cart in a class registered with `AddSingleton`. What happens when many customers use the app at the same time?
options: ASP.NET Core creates one singleton per request scope, so each customer keeps a separate cart
All concurrent requests share one instance until the process stops, so carts leak between customers
The container creates one instance per thread, so carts mix only when two requests share a thread
The instance is shared, but ASP.NET Core resets its fields at the end of every request
explanation: An ASP.NET Core app is one long-running process, so a singleton lives until the process stops and every request gets the same instance. The first option describes the scoped lifetime (05/02), which you must ask for explicitly; `AddSingleton` never behaves that way, and nothing resets its fields between requests.

question: Every HTTP response of an API must carry a security header. Where does that behaviour belong in an ASP.NET Core app?
options: A `BackgroundService` that inspects each response after it is sent
An Options class bound from `appsettings.json` with the header values
Middleware in the request pipeline, registered in `Program.cs`
A singleton service that the container calls after every endpoint
explanation: Code that runs around every request is middleware (or an endpoint filter), added to the pipeline in `Program.cs`. The container only creates what something asks for; it never calls a registered service on its own, so the last option would do nothing. A `BackgroundService` runs outside the request and cannot change a response.

question: A program contains `int quantity = "10";`. What happens?
options: It compiles, and the assignment throws `InvalidCastException` when the line runs
It compiles, because the text holds digits and is converted to 10
It compiles with a warning, and the text is parsed with `int.Parse`
The build fails: `string` does not convert implicitly to `int`
explanation: C# checks types before the program runs, so the compiler reports CS0029 and no program is produced. The first option describes a check at run time; in C# the program never gets that far. Turning text into a number is an explicit step with `int.TryParse` or `int.Parse` (00/04).

question: You have written programs before and want to know whether to skip module 00. What does this track ask you to do?
options: Open the challenge of 00/07; if you solve it without help, start at module 01
Pass the quiz of 00/01; a passed quiz there unlocks module 01
Read every lesson of module 00 first, because module 01 stays locked until they are complete
Skip it whenever you know any programming language, since module 01 repeats the basics
explanation: The skip rule is one test: the 00/07 challenge, which combines what module 00 teaches: parsing text, loops over arrays, a dictionary, a class with a constructor and properties, and exceptions. Nothing in the track is locked, so the third option is wrong, and module 01 does not repeat the basics: it assumes them, which is why the last option leaves gaps that show up in 02/01.

question: An endpoint calls `File.ReadAllTextAsync(path).Result`. The code works on your laptop, but the API slows down badly under load in production. Why?
options: `.Result` makes every request wait on one shared synchronization context
Each blocked call holds a pool thread while waiting, so the pool runs out of threads
Async file APIs are slower than sync ones, so `File.ReadAllText` would fix it
The file is read again on every call; it should be cached in a static field
explanation: Blocking on a task keeps a shared thread busy doing nothing; with many concurrent requests the pool runs out of threads and requests queue. `await` releases the thread while the I/O runs. Switching to the synchronous API, the third option, still blocks a thread per request; ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, which rules out the first.

question: You find a C# answer online that uses a `Startup` class, `System.Web` and `web.config`. What should you conclude first?
options: It is the recommended structure for new .NET 10 APIs
It is current, but only for apps hosted in IIS rather than Kestrel
It was written for .NET Framework or early ASP.NET Core
It needs `<LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>` to compile on .NET 10
explanation: `System.Web` and `web.config` belong to .NET Framework, and a `Startup` class is the pre-.NET 6 ASP.NET Core pattern; current templates use top-level statements in `Program.cs`. The second option is tempting because `web.config` still appears when modern apps run behind IIS, but there it only configures the IIS module, and `System.Web` does not exist in modern .NET.
